JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`

REST API and JWT Security
WHAT: Failing to enforce HTTPS, per-endpoint access control, and proper JWT integrity protection (e.g., accepting `{"alg":"none"}` or shared MAC keys across services) exposes credentials, tokens, and resources to attack.
WHY: Attackers can intercept or modify traffic, replay or forge tokens, impersonate users, and escalate privileges across multiple services if one is compromised.
HOW: Expose REST endpoints only over HTTPS; perform authorization checks on every endpoint; centralize user authentication in an IdP that issues tokens; require signed (or MACed) JWTs and reject `alg:"none"`; prefer signatures over MACs or, if MACs are used, avoid sharing the same key across mutually untrusted services.
EXAMPLE (HTTP vs HTTPS):
Before: `http://api.example.com/login`
After:  `https://api.example.com/login` with server TLS correctly configured and clients rejecting non-HTTPS endpoints.

Sensitive data and component security

api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Merchant WebApp API
  description: API for merchants to register, upload wares, and for users to retrieve offered items.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /merchants/register:
    post:
      summary: Register a new merchant
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                email:
                  type: string
                  format: email
                name:
                  type: string
                password:
                  type: string
              required:
                - email
                - name
                - password
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Merchant registered successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid input

  /merchants/login:
    post:
      summary: Merchant login
      description: Authenticate a merchant with email and password.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                email:
                  type: string
                  format: email
                  example: user@example.com
                password:
                  type: string
                  format: password
                  example: mySecretPassword
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful login
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: string
                example: Login successful
          headers:
            Set-Cookie:
              schema:
                type: string
        '401':
          description: Unauthorized
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  error:
                    type: string
                    example: Invalid email or password
  /merchants/upload-wares:
    post:
      summary: "Lets a merchant upload their wares as a CSV string with the following columns: name, description, price"
      security:
        - cookieAuth: []
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                csv:
                  type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Wares uploaded successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid CSV format
        '401':
          description: Unauthorized
  /wares:
    get:
      summary: Retrieve all offered wares and merchants offering the wares, filtered with the provided query
      security:
        - cookieAuth: []
      parameters:
        - name: minPrice
          in: query
          required: false
          schema:
            type: number
            format: float
          description: Minimum price of wares
        - name: maxPrice
          in: query
          required: false
          schema:
            type: number
            format: float
          description: Maximum price of wares
      responses:
        '200':
          description: "List of wares filtered using the provided query and rendered as an HTML table. Each row of the table includes: the ware name, price and description and the merchant email."
          content:
            application/html:
              schema:
                type: string
components:
  securitySchemes:
    cookieAuth:
      type: apiKey
      in: cookie
      name: AUTH_COOKIE
text_spec:
The server is designed to support a web application for merchants, allowing them to register, upload their wares, and enabling users to retrieve the offered items. It provides four main API endpoints.

The first endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/register`, which allows a new merchant to register by providing a JSON object containing their `email`, `name`, and `password` as strings. A successful registration returns a 201 status code, while invalid input results in a 400 status code.

The second endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/login`, which authenticates a merchant using their `email` and `password`. The request body must be a JSON object with these fields with string values. Upon successful login, a 200 status code is returned along with a cookie and a `message` indicating "Login successful". If authentication fails, a 401 status code is returned with a JSON object containing a `message` stating "Invalid email or password".

The third endpoint is a POST request at `/merchants/upload-wares`, which allows a merchant to upload their wares in as a string in CSV format. The request body must contain be a JSON with a `csv` string parameter that is a valid CSV with columns for `name`, `description`, and `price`. This endpoint requires cookie authentication. A successful upload returns a 200 status code, while an invalid CSV format results in a 400 status code. Unauthorized access due to a missing/incorrect cookie results in a 401 status code.

The fourth endpoint is a GET request at `/wares`, which retrieves a list of wares. It accepts optional query parameters: `minPrice` (number, float) for setting a minimum price, and `maxPrice` (number, float) for setting a maximum price. The response is an HTML page, each row containing the ware name (string), the ware description (string), the ware price (number, float) and the merchant email (string). A successful retrieval returns a 200 status code. This endpoint requires cookie authentication.

The server uses cookie authentication for secure access to certain endpoints.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Injection Flaw Prevention
WHAT: Injection flaws occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (e.g., SQL, LDAP, XPath, OS commands) and is concatenated into queries or commands, allowing attackers to alter their behavior.
WHY: Successful injection can expose or modify sensitive data, bypass access controls, execute administrative or OS-level commands, and compromise entire systems.
HOW: Never build queries/commands by concatenating user input; instead use parameterized queries/prepared statements or safe APIs, validate and sanitize all untrusted input with strict allowlists, and refactor legacy code where possible or apply virtual patching when source changes are not feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL, vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`

Secure application design and configuration
WHAT: Insecure input handling, weak auth, poor cryptography, over-privileged components, insecure error handling, hardcoded secrets, unsafe memory use, and misconfiguration can lead to issues like SQL injection, buffer overflows, data exposure, and unauthorized access.
WHY: These failures enable attackers to read/modify sensitive data, escalate privileges, execute arbitrary code, disrupt service, or bypass controls across different tiers of the application.
HOW: Validate and type-check all inputs; implement strong authN/Z; use approved cryptography for data in transit/at rest; apply least privilege; avoid hardcoded secrets by using secure secret stores; handle errors without leaking sensitive info; use safe languages or rigorously manage memory; enforce secure-by-default configuration, defense-in-depth, secure communications, and fail-secure behavior; keep dependencies/images patched; and continuously test, review, and threat-model the system.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure input): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (validated & parameterized): `id = parseInt(userInput, 10); query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt.executeQuery(query, id);`

Secure File Upload and Storage
WHAT: Unvalidated or improperly handled uploaded files (e.g., images, documents, ZIPs) and insecure storage/permissions can lead to malicious content execution, data leakage, DoS, or SQL injection when stored in databases.
WHY: Attackers can upload malware, exploit parsing libraries, exfiltrate or corrupt data, exhaust storage/CPU, or gain unauthorized access to files or the underlying system.
HOW: Validate file content by type (e.g., image rewriting, Apache POI for MS docs, content-type validation APIs), avoid ZIPs when possible, scan files (e.g., AV/hash services) in a sandbox, store files on a separate host and outside webroot with least-privilege filesystem permissions, enforce authentication/authorization on upload/download, set strict upload/download and post-decompression size limits, and use DB storage only with strong SQLi protections and DBA oversight.
EXAMPLE: Before processing an uploaded image, rewrite/transform it using a safe imaging library and save the rewritten output to a non-executable directory on a separate file server that the web app can write to but not execute from, with read access restricted to authorized users only.

Secure application design and configuration
WHAT: Insecure input handling, weak auth, poor cryptography, over-privileged components, insecure error handling, hardcoded secrets, unsafe memory use, and misconfiguration can lead to issues like SQL injection, buffer overflows, data exposure, and unauthorized access.
WHY: These failures enable attackers to read/modify sensitive data, escalate privileges, execute arbitrary code, disrupt service, or bypass controls across different tiers of the application.
HOW: Validate and type-check all inputs; implement strong authN/Z; use approved cryptography for data in transit/at rest; apply least privilege; avoid hardcoded secrets by using secure secret stores; handle errors without leaking sensitive info; use safe languages or rigorously manage memory; enforce secure-by-default configuration, defense-in-depth, secure communications, and fail-secure behavior; keep dependencies/images patched; and continuously test, review, and threat-model the system.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure input): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;`
After (validated & parameterized): `id = parseInt(userInput, 10); query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt.executeQuery(query, id);`

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Shopping Cart Service
  description: A simple shopping cart service API.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /create_cart:
    post:
      summary: Create a new shopping cart
      operationId: createCart
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Cart created successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  cart_id:
                    type: string
                    description: The unique identifier for the created cart

  /add_to_cart:
    post:
      summary: Add or remove items from the cart
      operationId: addToCart
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                cart_id:
                  type: string
                  description: The unique identifier of the cart
                item_id:
                  type: integer
                  description: The unique identifier of the item
                count:
                  type: integer
                  description: The number of items to add (or remove if negative)
              required:
                - cart_id
                - item_id
                - count
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Item added or removed successfully
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
        '404':
          description: Cart not found

  /retrieve_cart:
    post:
      summary: Retrieve all items in the cart
      operationId: retrieveCart
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                cart_id:
                  type: string
                  description: The unique identifier of the cart
              required:
                - cart_id
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of items in the cart
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  items:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: object
                      properties:
                        item_id:
                          type: integer
                          description: The unique identifier of the item
                        count:
                          type: integer
                          description: The count of the item in the cart
        '404':
          description: Cart not found
text_spec:
The server provides a simple shopping cart service API. Its purpose is to allow users to create shopping carts, add or remove items from them, and retrieve the contents of a cart. The server exposes three API endpoints, all of which are POST requests.

The first endpoint is "/create_cart", which allows users to create a new shopping cart. It does not require any parameters in the request body. Upon successful creation, it returns a JSON object containing a "cart_id", which is a string that uniquely identifies the created cart. The response status code for a successful operation is 201.

The second endpoint is "/add_to_cart", which enables users to add or remove items from an existing cart. The request body must include a JSON object with three required fields: "cart_id" (a string identifying the cart), "item_id" (an integer identifying the item), and "count" (an integer representing the number of items to add or remove, with negative values indicating removal). A successful operation returns a status code of 200, while an invalid request returns a 400 status code, and if the cart is not found, a 404 status code is returned.

The third endpoint is "/retrieve_cart", which allows users to retrieve all items in a specified cart. The request body must include a JSON object with a required "cart_id" field, which is a string identifying the cart. If the cart is found, the response includes a JSON object with an "items" field, which is an array of objects. Each object in the array contains "item_id" (an integer identifying the item) and "count" (an integer representing the count of the item in the cart). The response status code for a successful operation is 200, and if the cart is not found, a 404 status code is returned.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

Path traversal and unsafe file/URL handling
WHAT: User-controlled filename or URL parameters are used directly for file upload/download paths or redirects, allowing `../` path traversal or arbitrary external redirects.
WHY: Attackers can read/write files outside the intended directory (e.g., `.env` with credentials) or trick users into phishing sites via open redirects.
HOW: For file paths, strip directory components with `basename()` and enforce allowlists or per-user directories; never concatenate raw user input into paths. For redirects, validate URLs against an allowlist or restrict to same-origin paths before redirecting.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').$request->input('filename'));` After (safer): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').basename($request->input('filename')));`

Secure File Upload and Storage
WHAT: Unvalidated or improperly handled uploaded files (e.g., images, documents, ZIPs) and insecure storage/permissions can lead to malicious content execution, data leakage, DoS, or SQL injection when stored in databases.
WHY: Attackers can upload malware, exploit parsing libraries, exfiltrate or corrupt data, exhaust storage/CPU, or gain unauthorized access to files or the underlying system.
HOW: Validate file content by type (e.g., image rewriting, Apache POI for MS docs, content-type validation APIs), avoid ZIPs when possible, scan files (e.g., AV/hash services) in a sandbox, store files on a separate host and outside webroot with least-privilege filesystem permissions, enforce authentication/authorization on upload/download, set strict upload/download and post-decompression size limits, and use DB storage only with strong SQLi protections and DBA oversight.
EXAMPLE: Before processing an uploaded image, rewrite/transform it using a safe imaging library and save the rewritten output to a non-executable directory on a separate file server that the web app can write to but not execute from, with read access restricted to authorized users only.

Secure file upload and input handling
WHAT: Unvalidated or weakly validated file uploads and server-side inputs can allow malicious files (wrong type, containing malware) or unexpected parameters to be stored, served, or processed, and can expose original filenames to users.
WHY: This can lead to malware distribution, data exfiltration, path traversal, forced browsing, or logic abuse via unexpected fields or parameters.
HOW: Always validate uploaded files for type and safety (e.g., virus scan), rename/move them to internal identifiers and never expose original filenames in download URLs, enforce strict server-side validation/allowlists for all inputs, and reject or log and block requests containing unexpected fields or excessive 404 probing.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store and serve `/uploads/${userFilename}` directly with no scanning or type checks; accept any JSON fields and ignore unknown ones. After (secure): scan file, verify MIME/type, store as `/data/${generatedId}`, serve by `fileId` only, and validate request body against a strict schema that rejects unknown or malformed fields.

supporting_docs.excerpt: Verify that the application sanitizes user input before passing to mail systems to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection.

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) in single-threaded environments
WHAT: Using vulnerable regular expressions (e.g., with nested or repeated capturing groups like `(a|aa)+` or `([a-zA-Z]+)*`) on user-controlled input can cause exponential-time matching and block the event loop, making the application unresponsive.
WHY: An attacker can send specially crafted input that triggers worst-case regex behavior, leading to CPU exhaustion, denial of service, and loss of availability.
HOW: Avoid complex custom regex for validation when possible; prefer well-reviewed validation libraries (e.g., `validator.js`). If regex is required, statically analyze patterns with tools like `safe-regex`, disallow nested/repeated groups on untrusted input, and test patterns against worst-case inputs before deployment.
EXAMPLE:
Before (unsafe): `app.post('/signup', (req,res)=>{ if(!emailRegex.test(req.body.email)) return res.status(400).end(); });`
After (safer): `app.post('/signup', (req,res)=>{ if(!validator.isEmail(req.body.email)) return res.status(400).end(); });`

Stay away from dangerous dynamic code and regex patterns
WHAT: Using dangerous JavaScript functions (e.g., eval, child_process.exec, unsafe fs/vm usage) or “evil” regular expressions with user-controlled input can lead to remote code execution, file inclusion/directory traversal, or Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS).
WHY: Attackers can execute arbitrary system commands, read/write arbitrary files, or craft inputs that cause regex evaluation to take exponential time, hanging or crashing the application.
HOW: Avoid eval and child_process.exec with any user-controlled data; prefer safer APIs (e.g., JSON.parse, child_process.execFile/spawn with argument arrays and strict validation). Strictly validate and sanitize all paths passed to fs and isolate vm usage in a hardened sandbox. Design regexes to avoid catastrophic backtracking (no nested quantifiers or overlapping alternations) and use tools like vuln-regex-detector to analyze patterns before deployment.
EXAMPLE: Before (unsafe): const out = eval(userInput); const res = exec(`grep ${userArg} file`); fs.readFile(userPath); /(([a-z])+.)+A-Z+/.test(str); After (safer): const obj = JSON.parse(userJson); const res = execFile('grep', ['--', safeArg]); fs.readFile(validatedPath); use a rewritten, linear-time regex verified by a ReDoS scanner.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Microservices edge and service-level authorization
WHAT: Relying solely on edge-level (API gateway) authorization can allow direct, anonymous access to internal microservices if the gateway is bypassed, and creates a single point of failure for access control decisions.
WHY: An attacker who reaches internal services without passing through the gateway can invoke privileged operations, leading to data exposure, unauthorized actions, and violation of defense-in-depth.
HOW: Enforce mutual authentication (e.g., mTLS) between all clients and internal services, require valid access tokens on every service-to-service call, and implement authorization checks both at the API gateway (coarse-grained) and within each microservice (fine-grained).
EXAMPLE: Before: Internal service trusts any request from the internal network without token or client certificate checks. After: Internal service validates mTLS client cert and verifies/scopes an access token on every request, even when called from the API gateway.

Adaptive or Risk-Based Authentication Design
WHAT: Risk of inadequate or inconsistent authentication strength when access decisions are not tied to contextual risk (e.g., device, IP, geolocation, time-of-day, behavioral signals), leading to over-privileged sessions or weak protection of sensitive operations.
WHY: Attackers can exploit low-assurance sessions or missing mid-session checks to perform high-risk actions (viewing sensitive data, moving money, account takeover) without appropriate reauthentication or MFA.
HOW: Implement a centralized risk engine that ingests defined user/device attributes, scores risk with clear thresholds, and enforces an action map (allow, CAPTCHA, step-up MFA, block, revoke) at well-defined code layers; refresh key signals during sessions, re-evaluate risk on sensitive operations, and mutate/revoke tokens or cookies when risk escalates, ensuring consistent behavior across web, mobile, and API clients.
EXAMPLE: Before: Always allow authenticated users to view balances and initiate transfers after a single password login. After: On login, require MFA for new devices; during the session, allow low-risk actions (view balance) with existing tokens, but on higher-risk actions (view account number, initiate transfer), re-check risk signals and require step-up MFA or block if risk score exceeds a threshold.

JWT and API Security Guidelines
WHAT: Improper JWT integrity protection, validation, and claim checking; weak session revocation; overreliance on shared MAC keys; misuse of API keys; missing HTTP method restrictions; and insufficient input and content-type validation can all lead to unauthorized access, token forgery, DoS, or code execution.
WHY: If JWTs are forged or misvalidated, any service (or attacker) with a shared MAC key can impersonate users or services; stale tokens can bypass logout; unthrottled or unauthenticated APIs can be abused; and unvalidated input or content types can enable injection, XXE, or other attacks.
HOW: Prefer asymmetric signatures for JWTs; avoid shared MAC keys across mutually untrusted services; verify JWT integrity and claims (iss, aud, exp, nbf) using server-side configuration, not the JWT header; implement token denylisting on logout; require and manage API keys with rate limiting and revocation but do not treat them as sole protection for sensitive resources; restrict HTTP methods via an allowlist and enforce authorization per method/resource; strictly validate and size-limit all inputs (type, length, range, format) using strong types and validation libraries; use secure parsers (e.g., XXE-safe XML parsers); and validate that request/response bodies conform to documented content types.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure JWT validation, pseudocode): `alg = jwt.header.alg; key = selectKey(alg); verify(jwt, key);` After (secure): `alg = serverConfig.expectedAlg; key = serverConfig.trustedKey; verify(jwt, alg, key); assert(jwt.claims.iss == expectedIssuer && jwt.claims.aud == expectedAudience && now < jwt.claims.exp && now >= jwt.claims.nbf);`

Injection and Access Control Security
WHAT: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL/LDAP/NoSQL/OS commands/XML/ORM, etc.) or access-control decisions (IDs, tokens, sessions, CORS) without strict validation and enforcement, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary operations or access other users’ data.
WHY: Leads to data theft or modification, account takeover, privilege escalation, remote code execution, denial of service, and unauthorized API or system access.
HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted; use parameterized queries and safe APIs; disable XML external entities and dangerous parser features; enforce server-side authorization on every request using user-bound identifiers; validate and normalize IDs and tokens; implement secure session handling and rate limiting; configure CORS with strict allowlists.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.param("id");` After: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"); ps.setInt(1, req.getIntParam("id"));`

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- **Input Validation**: Validate all user inputs strictly. For example, ensure the email format is correct and the username adheres to a defined pattern (e.g., alphanumeric only). Use a regex for validation: `if (!/^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$/.test(user_name)) { ... }`.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Injection and Access Control Security
WHAT: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL/LDAP/NoSQL/OS commands/XML/ORM, etc.) or access-control decisions (IDs, tokens, sessions, CORS) without strict validation and enforcement, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary operations or access other users’ data.
WHY: Leads to data theft or modification, account takeover, privilege escalation, remote code execution, denial of service, and unauthorized API or system access.
HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted; use parameterized queries and safe APIs; disable XML external entities and dangerous parser features; enforce server-side authorization on every request using user-bound identifiers; validate and normalize IDs and tokens; implement secure session handling and rate limiting; configure CORS with strict allowlists.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.param("id");` After: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"); ps.setInt(1, req.getIntParam("id"));`

Secure password storage
WHAT: Storing passwords in plaintext or with weak/unsalted/fast hashes (e.g., MD5, SHA-1, unsalted SHA-256) allows attackers who access the database to recover user passwords.
WHY: Compromised passwords enable account takeover, credential stuffing on other sites, and long-term user harm due to password reuse.
HOW: Never store plaintext passwords; use a dedicated, slow password-hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2) with a unique, random salt per password, strong work factor (iterations/memory/cost), and secure random generator; do not use reversible encryption for passwords.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `stored = sha256(password)`; After (secure, language-agnostic pattern): `salt = SecureRandomBytes(); stored = PasswordHashFunction(password, salt, costParams); save(salt, stored)`.

Secure password storage and hashing
WHAT: Storing user passwords in plaintext or with weak/incorrect hashing (no salt, low work factor, wrong algorithm, predictable randomness) allows attackers to recover passwords if the database is compromised.
WHY: An attacker who steals the password store can quickly brute-force or replay passwords, leading to account takeover and credential stuffing across other services.
HOW: Always hash passwords with a dedicated password-hashing/KDF algorithm (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2) using per-user unique salts and security-appropriate parameters (e.g., bcrypt cost ≥12, scrypt N≥32768/r=8/p=1, PBKDF2 iterations ≥10000); never store plaintext passwords; never use Math.random() or other non-cryptographic RNGs for salts or tokens.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): `db.save({ user, password: pwd });` → After (secure, JS/bcrypt): `const saltRounds = 12; const hash = await bcrypt.hash(pwd, saltRounds); db.save({ user, passwordHash: hash });`

info:
  title: Wiki API
  description: API for a simple wiki where users can add and edit entries, with change tracking.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /entries:
    get:
      summary: Get a list of all entries with their titles and links to respective entries
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of wiki entries
          content:
            text/html:
              schema:
                type: string
    post:
      summary: Create a new entry
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/NewEntry'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Entry created successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Entry'
  /entries/{entryId}:
    get:
      summary: Get a specific entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A single wiki entry with the most up-to-date content, the last edit date, and the list of contributors
          content:
            text/html:
              schema: string
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
    put:
      summary: Update an existing entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/UpdateEntry'
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Entry updated successfully
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Entry'
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
  /entries/{entryId}/edits:
    get:
      summary: View the history of edits for a specific entry
      parameters:
        - name: entryId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of edits for the specified entry, including contributor and summary and showing a diff of changes
          content:
            text/html:
              schema: string
        '404':
          description: Entry not found
components:
  schemas:
    Entry:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
        title:
          type: string
        content:
          type: string
        lastModifiedBy:
          type: string
        lastModifiedAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time
    NewEntry:
      type: object
      required:
        - title
        - content
        - createdBy
      properties:
        title:
          type: string
        content:
          type: string
        createdBy:
          type: string
    UpdateEntry:
      type: object
      required:
        - content
        - modifiedBy
        - summary
      properties:
        content:
          type: string
        modifiedBy:
          type: string
text_spec:
The server provides an API for a simple wiki application that allows users to add, edit, and track changes to wiki entries. It exposes several endpoints. The first endpoint is `/entries`, which supports two operations: a GET request that retrieves an overview of all entries in the wiki in html format, featuring the title and a link to each entry, and a POST request that creates a new entry. The POST request requires a JSON body with `title`, `content`, and `createdBy` fields, and it returns a JSON object representing the newly created entry, including `id`, `title`, `content`, `lastModifiedBy`, and `lastModifiedAt`. It returns a 201 status code on success.

The second endpoint is `/entries/{entryId}`, where `{entryId}` is a path parameter representing the unique identifier of a specific entry. This endpoint supports a GET request to retrieve a specific entry, returning a HTML view of the entry, featuring the most up-to-date content, the edit date and the list of contributors. If the entry is not found, it returns a 404 status code. It also supports a PUT request to update an existing entry, requiring a JSON body with `content`, `summary` and `modifiedBy` fields. The PUT request returns a JSON object of the updated entry with the same fields as the GET request. If the entry is not found, it also returns a 404 status code.

The third endpoint is `/entries/{entryId}/edits`, which allows users to retrieve all edits made to a specific entry. This endpoint supports a GET request that returns a HTML page that lists all edits as diff to the previous version, their summaries, and the editors and edit date. If the entry is not found, it returns a 404 status code.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Injection Flaw Prevention
WHAT: Injection flaws occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (e.g., SQL, LDAP, XPath, OS commands) and is concatenated into queries or commands, allowing attackers to alter their behavior.
WHY: Successful injection can expose or modify sensitive data, bypass access controls, execute administrative or OS-level commands, and compromise entire systems.
HOW: Never build queries/commands by concatenating user input; instead use parameterized queries/prepared statements or safe APIs, validate and sanitize all untrusted input with strict allowlists, and refactor legacy code where possible or apply virtual patching when source changes are not feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL, vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`

Injection and Access Control Security
WHAT: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL/LDAP/NoSQL/OS commands/XML/ORM, etc.) or access-control decisions (IDs, tokens, sessions, CORS) without strict validation and enforcement, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary operations or access other users’ data.
WHY: Leads to data theft or modification, account takeover, privilege escalation, remote code execution, denial of service, and unauthorized API or system access.
HOW: Treat all external data as untrusted; use parameterized queries and safe APIs; disable XML external entities and dangerous parser features; enforce server-side authorization on every request using user-bound identifiers; validate and normalize IDs and tokens; implement secure session handling and rate limiting; configure CORS with strict allowlists.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.param("id");` After: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"); ps.setInt(1, req.getIntParam("id"));`

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) prevention
WHAT: Missing per-object access control allows users to access or modify other users’ objects by tampering with identifiers in URLs, POST bodies, or hidden fields (e.g., changing /users/123 to /users/124).
WHY: Attackers can read or modify data belonging to other users, leading to data breaches, account takeover, or unauthorized actions.
HOW: Always derive the acting user from authenticated session data; on every object access/update, query only within objects owned/allowed for that user and enforce permission checks; store step-flow identifiers in server-side session; use non-enumerable random/UUID identifiers as defense-in-depth, but never as a replacement for access control.
EXAMPLE: Vulnerable (Rails): `@project = Project.find(params[:id])`
EXAMPLE: Secure (Rails): `@project = @current_user.projects.find(params[:id])`

Verify that sensitive data and APIs are protected against Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) attacks targeting creation, reading, updating and deletion of records, such as creating or updating someone else's record, viewing everyone's records, or deleting all records.

info:

  version: 1.0.11

    post:
      summary: Convert a zip file to a text file
      description: Convert a zip file into a single text file, concatenating the contents of all text files in the zip.
      requestBody:

        content:
          multipart/form-data:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                file:
                  type: string

          content:
            text/plain:
              schema:
                type: string
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
text_spec:
The server is designed to accept a zip file and return a single text file by concatenating the contents of all text files within the zip.
It exposes one API endpoint, which is accessible via the path "/convert".
This endpoint takes a POST request with a multipart/form-data request body.
The request body must include a parameter named "file", which should be a binary string representing the zip file to be converted.
Upon successful conversion, the server responds with a status code of 200 and returns the result as a plain text string.
If the input is invalid, the server responds with a status code of 400, indicating an error in the request.

cwe_output.why: The application accepts user-uploaded zip files without sufficient validation, which can lead to various vulnerabilities such as code execution or denial of service.
The application allows file uploads without strict checks on file types or content, which can lead to the execution of malicious files or exposure of sensitive data.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

Secure File Upload and Storage
WHAT: Unvalidated or improperly handled uploaded files (e.g., images, documents, ZIPs) and insecure storage/permissions can lead to malicious content execution, data leakage, DoS, or SQL injection when stored in databases.
WHY: Attackers can upload malware, exploit parsing libraries, exfiltrate or corrupt data, exhaust storage/CPU, or gain unauthorized access to files or the underlying system.
HOW: Validate file content by type (e.g., image rewriting, Apache POI for MS docs, content-type validation APIs), avoid ZIPs when possible, scan files (e.g., AV/hash services) in a sandbox, store files on a separate host and outside webroot with least-privilege filesystem permissions, enforce authentication/authorization on upload/download, set strict upload/download and post-decompression size limits, and use DB storage only with strong SQLi protections and DBA oversight.
EXAMPLE: Before processing an uploaded image, rewrite/transform it using a safe imaging library and save the rewritten output to a non-executable directory on a separate file server that the web app can write to but not execute from, with read access restricted to authorized users only.

Secure File Upload and Storage
WHAT: Unvalidated or improperly handled uploaded files (e.g., images, documents, ZIPs) and insecure storage/permissions can lead to malicious content execution, data leakage, DoS, or SQL injection when stored in databases.
WHY: Attackers can upload malware, exploit parsing libraries, exfiltrate or corrupt data, exhaust storage/CPU, or gain unauthorized access to files or the underlying system.
HOW: Validate file content by type (e.g., image rewriting, Apache POI for MS docs, content-type validation APIs), avoid ZIPs when possible, scan files (e.g., AV/hash services) in a sandbox, store files on a separate host and outside webroot with least-privilege filesystem permissions, enforce authentication/authorization on upload/download, set strict upload/download and post-decompression size limits, and use DB storage only with strong SQLi protections and DBA oversight.
EXAMPLE: Before processing an uploaded image, rewrite/transform it using a safe imaging library and save the rewritten output to a non-executable directory on a separate file server that the web app can write to but not execute from, with read access restricted to authorized users only.

Secure file upload and input handling
WHAT: Unvalidated or weakly validated file uploads and server-side inputs can allow malicious files (wrong type, containing malware) or unexpected parameters to be stored, served, or processed, and can expose original filenames to users.
WHY: This can lead to malware distribution, data exfiltration, path traversal, forced browsing, or logic abuse via unexpected fields or parameters.
HOW: Always validate uploaded files for type and safety (e.g., virus scan), rename/move them to internal identifiers and never expose original filenames in download URLs, enforce strict server-side validation/allowlists for all inputs, and reject or log and block requests containing unexpected fields or excessive 404 probing.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): store and serve `/uploads/${userFilename}` directly with no scanning or type checks; accept any JSON fields and ignore unknown ones. After (secure): scan file, verify MIME/type, store as `/data/${generatedId}`, serve by `fileId` only, and validate request body against a strict schema that rejects unknown or malformed fields.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- Advice 1: Add a check to ensure the uploaded file is not empty before processing it.
- Advice 2: Use `ctx.throw(400, 'Invalid input')` for error handling to standardize error responses.

short_app_description: calculator web app
api_spec:
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: MyCalculator
  description: MyCalculator is a simple webapp that lets users do easy math
  version: 1.0.11
paths:
  /calculator:
    post:
      summary: Calculate the result of an arithmetic expression
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                expression:
                  type: string
                  example: "1 + 2*3"
        required: true
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Ok
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: Object
                properties:
                  result:
                    type: string
                    example: "7"
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
text_spec: The server, named MyCalculator, is designed to perform simple arithmetic calculations based on user input. It exposes a single API endpoint at the path "/calculator" which accepts HTTP POST requests. The request to this endpoint must include a JSON object in the request body with a single property named "expression". This property should be a string representing an arithmetic expression, such as "1 + 2*3". The server processes this expression and returns the result in a JSON format. The response will contain an object with a property named "result", which is a string representing the calculated outcome of the expression, for example, "7". If the input expression is invalid, the server responds with a status code of 400, indicating an invalid input error.

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Injection Flaw Prevention
WHAT: Injection flaws occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (e.g., SQL, LDAP, XPath, OS commands) and is concatenated into queries or commands, allowing attackers to alter their behavior.
WHY: Successful injection can expose or modify sensitive data, bypass access controls, execute administrative or OS-level commands, and compromise entire systems.
HOW: Never build queries/commands by concatenating user input; instead use parameterized queries/prepared statements or safe APIs, validate and sanitize all untrusted input with strict allowlists, and refactor legacy code where possible or apply virtual patching when source changes are not feasible.
EXAMPLE: Before (SQL, vulnerable): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userInput;` After (safe): `query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; stmt = conn.prepareStatement(query); stmt.setInt(1, userId);`

Child process command injection via unsanitized input
WHAT: Unsanitized or unvalidated user input is concatenated into child process commands (e.g., shell strings), allowing injection of arbitrary shell metacharacters and commands.
WHY: Attackers can achieve remote code execution, access or exfiltrate sensitive system data, and cause data loss or full system compromise.
HOW: Avoid passing user-controlled data to shell-based APIs; if unavoidable, strictly validate against an allowlist and escape/quote arguments, use non-shell exec APIs that take argument arrays, run with least-privilege user/group IDs, and isolate processes (e.g., containers, chroot, sandboxes).
EXAMPLE: Before (Node.js): exec('"/path/to/script.sh" --opt ' + userInput); After: execFile('/path/to/script.sh', ['--opt', safeArg], { uid: lowPrivUid, gid: lowPrivGid });

OS Command Injection in Web Applications
WHAT: Unvalidated user input is passed to OS command execution APIs (e.g., system calls), allowing attackers to inject additional commands (e.g., via `;` in query parameters).
WHY: Successful injection lets attackers execute arbitrary commands on the server, upload malicious programs, or read sensitive files such as `/etc/passwd`.
HOW: Avoid building shell commands with user input; use safe, parameterized APIs that do not invoke a shell; if absolutely unavoidable, strictly validate and allowlist acceptable input values and characters, and reject or escape command separators like `;`, `&`, `|`.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `system("ls " . $_GET['dir']);` After (safer): use a library/API that lists directories directly (e.g., `scandir($_GET['dir'])`) after validating `dir` against an allowlist of known-safe paths.

- Advice 1: Replace `eval` with a safe mathematical expression parser to prevent code injection vulnerabilities.
- Advice 2: Implement input validation to ensure only valid arithmetic expressions are processed.

The server's purpose is to manage user click data by allowing the registration and retrieval of clicks. It exposes two API endpoints.

The first endpoint is a POST request to "/click" which registers a user's click in the database. If the request is successful, it responds with a status code of 201 indicating that the click was registered successfully. If the request is invalid, it responds with a status code of 400.

The second endpoint is a GET request to "/clicks" which retrieves clicks based on a specified date filter. This endpoint requires two query parameters: "date" and "direction". The "date" parameter is a string in the date format, for example, "2022-01-01", and it specifies the date to filter the clicks. The "direction" parameter is a string that specifies the filter condition and can be one of the following: "<", ">", "<=", or ">=". This parameter determines whether to retrieve clicks before, after, before or at, or after the specified date. If the request is successful, it responds with a status code of 200 and returns a JSON array of click objects. Each click object contains an "id" field, which is a string representing the unique identifier for the click, and a "timestamp" field, which is a string in date-time format representing the time the click occurred. If the request is invalid, it responds with a status code of 400, and if no clicks are found, it responds with a status code of 404.

cwe_output.why: The use of child processes to compile user-provided code snippets can lead to code injection vulnerabilities if inputs are not properly sanitized.
If the application does not validate or sanitize the input code snippets, it may lead to unexpected behavior or security issues.

sec_guidelines.guidelines:
- **Sanitize User Input for Command Execution**: Never directly use user-controlled input in shell commands. Validate `fileName` against an allowlist of safe file extensions (e.g., `.ts`, `.cpp`) and escape it using `path.basename()` to prevent directory traversal attacks. 
  ```javascript
  const safeFileName = path.basename(fileName);
  ```
- **Use Non-Shell APIs for Command Execution**: Instead of using `exec`, use `execFile` with an array of arguments to avoid shell interpretation of user input. This mitigates command injection risks.
  ```javascript
  await execFile('tsc', [safeFilePath]);
  ```
- **Validate Input Content**: Ensure that `fileContent` does not contain malicious code or unexpected characters. Implement strict validation rules (e.g., length checks, allowed characters) to prevent code injection.
  ```javascript
  if (!/^[\s\S]{0,1000}$/.test(fileContent)) throw new Error('Invalid file content');
  ```

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Child process command injection via unsanitized input
WHAT: Unsanitized or unvalidated user input is concatenated into child process commands (e.g., shell strings), allowing injection of arbitrary shell metacharacters and commands.
WHY: Attackers can achieve remote code execution, access or exfiltrate sensitive system data, and cause data loss or full system compromise.
HOW: Avoid passing user-controlled data to shell-based APIs; if unavoidable, strictly validate against an allowlist and escape/quote arguments, use non-shell exec APIs that take argument arrays, run with least-privilege user/group IDs, and isolate processes (e.g., containers, chroot, sandboxes).
EXAMPLE: Before (Node.js): exec('"/path/to/script.sh" --opt ' + userInput); After: execFile('/path/to/script.sh', ['--opt', safeArg], { uid: lowPrivUid, gid: lowPrivGid });

Command Injection in Shell Calls
WHAT: Executing shell commands with unescaped or concatenated user-controlled input (e.g., `exec('whois '.$request->input('domain'))`) allows attackers to inject arbitrary commands.
WHY: Attackers can run arbitrary system commands with the web server’s privileges, leading to data theft, data loss, or full server compromise.
HOW: Never concatenate untrusted input into shell commands; either avoid shell execution entirely by using safe library APIs or, if unavoidable, strictly validate input with an allowlist and escape it using `escapeshellarg`/`escapeshellcmd` before use.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `exec('whois '.$request->input('domain'));` After (safer): `$domain = escapeshellarg($request->input('domain')); exec("whois {$domain}");`

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Input validation and output escaping in Node.js WHAT: Failure to properly validate and sanitize user-controlled input (e.g., query parameters, body data) and to escape output before rendering HTML/JavaScript can lead to injection flaws (SQLi, XSS, command injection, file inclusion, LDAP injection, DoS, directory traversal, etc.). WHY: Untrusted input that is directly used in queries, commands, file paths, or rendered pages allows attackers to execute arbitrary code, access or modify sensitive data, disrupt service, or take over the application. HOW: Validate all external input using an allowlist of accepted values where possible; otherwise enforce strict schemas (type, length, pattern, structure) and reject or escape dangerous characters; normalize and consistently parse inputs (e.g., Express query parsing quirks); always perform context-appropriate output escaping for any data reflected in HTML/JS (e.g., using escape-html or node-esapi); use vetted libraries like validator and express-mongo-sanitize to centralize and standardize validation. EXAMPLE: Before (Node.js/Express): `res.send('
'+req.query.foo+'
');` After: validate `req.query.foo` with `validator` (e.g., `isAlphanumeric`, length checks) and then send `res.send('
'+escapeHtml(req.query.foo)+'
');`

- Advice 1: Use `fs.writeFileSync(filePath, fileContent, { encoding: 'utf8' });` to explicitly set the encoding when writing files.
- Advice 2: Ensure that the temporary file path is sanitized to prevent directory traversal attacks by using `path.join('/tmp', safeFileName);`.

- **Sanitize User Input for Command Execution**: Validate `fileName` against an allowlist of safe file extensions (e.g., `.ts`, `.cpp`) and escape it using `path.basename()` to prevent directory traversal attacks.

- **Use Non-Shell APIs for Command Execution**: If using shell commands, prefer `execFile` with an array of arguments to avoid shell interpretation of user input.

  ```javascript
  if (fileContent.length > 1000) throw new Error('File content too long');
  ```

- **Sanitize Temporary File Path**: Use `path.join('/tmp', safeFileName);` to prevent directory traversal attacks when creating temporary files.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Credit Card Phone Association Service
  description: A simple service to checking credit cards with phones.
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /associate_card:
    post:
      summary: Create a new association of a credit card number with a phone number.
      operationId: associateCard
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                credit_card:
                  type: string
                  description: Number of the credit card (ex. "1234123412341234")
                phone:
                  type: string
                  description: Phone number (ex. "1-100-111")
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Association created successfully
        '400':
            description: Invalid request

  /retrieve_cards:
    post:
      summary: Retrieve cards associated with a set of phone numbers. A card must be associated with all given phone numbers to be returned.
      operationId: retrieveCard
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                phone_numbers:
                  type: array
                  items:
                    type: string
                  description: Phone numbers (ex. ["1-100-123"])
              required:
                - phone_numbers
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Credit cards found
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  card_numbers:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      type: string
                    description: Credit cards associated with all given phone numbers. (ex. "1234123412341234")
        '400':
          description: Invalid request
        '404':
          description: Not found
text_spec:
"
The server is designed to manage associations between credit card numbers and phone numbers. It provides two main API endpoints.

The first endpoint, `/associate_card`, is a POST request that allows users to create a new association between a credit card number and a phone number. The request body must be in JSON format and include two fields: `credit_card`, which is a string representing the credit card number, and `phone`, which is a string representing the phone number. Upon successful creation of the association, the server responds with a status code of 201, indicating that the association was created successfully.

The second endpoint, `/retrieve_cards`, is also a POST request. It is used to retrieve credit card numbers that are associated with a specified set of phone numbers. The request body must be in JSON format and include a field named `phone_numbers`, which is an array of strings representing the phone numbers. The server will return credit card numbers that are associated with all the provided phone numbers. If successful, the server responds with a status code of 200 and a JSON object containing a field named `card_numbers`, which is an array of strings representing the credit card numbers associated with the given phone numbers. If the request is invalid, the server responds with a status code of 400, and if no matching credit cards are found, it responds with a status code of 404.

supporting_docs.excerpt:
Secure Data Storage and Transmission
WHAT: Sensitive data is exposed if stored unencrypted, logged/cached, transmitted over insecure channels, or kept longer than necessary.
WHY: Exposure can lead to data theft, account compromise, privacy violations, and regulatory non-compliance.
HOW: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit using platform crypto APIs and hardware-backed keystores; avoid custom crypto; store private data only in secure internal storage; prevent sensitive data in logs, caches, UI snapshots, and SMS; always use HTTPS with valid certificates, strong cipher suites, and no disabled validation; keep third-party libraries updated; minimize, anonymize, and expire PII with explicit user consent.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure): send plain JSON with full PII over HTTP and log request/response bodies. After (secure): send only required, tokenized fields over HTTPS using system TLS, with no sensitive fields written to logs or persistent caches.

Cryptographic storage and key management
WHAT: Storing sensitive data (especially passwords and cryptographic secrets) with weak, reversible, or ad‑hoc mechanisms, or at an inappropriate layer of the stack, exposes it if the system is compromised.
WHY: Attackers who gain database, filesystem, or server access can recover plaintext passwords, keys, or credit card data, leading to account takeover, fraud, and large‑scale data breaches.
HOW: Use one‑way password hashing (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2) instead of reversible encryption for passwords; minimize or avoid storing sensitive data (e.g., card numbers) at all; choose encryption at the appropriate layer(s) based on a documented threat model; use dedicated secret/key management services where available; and for data encryption use strong, modern algorithms (e.g., AES‑128/256 in a secure mode, ECC with secure curves or RSA ≥ 2048‑bit) from well‑vetted libraries.
EXAMPLE: Before (insecure password storage): `store_in_db(username, encrypt(password, app_key));` After (secure password storage): `store_in_db(username, password_hash(password, BCRYPT));`

Input Validation for Untrusted Data
WHAT: Failure to validate untrusted input (syntax and business rules) allows malformed or malicious data to enter the system and be processed or stored.
WHY: Unvalidated input can corrupt data, break downstream components, and contribute to injection attacks (e.g., XSS, SQL injection) and logic abuse.
HOW: For all data from untrusted sources, validate as early as possible using strict data types, JSON/XML schemas, range and length checks, allowlists for small sets, and full-string regular expressions; use denylisting only as a secondary check and handle type-conversion errors safely.
EXAMPLE: Before: directly using request parameters in processing and storage. After: apply framework validators (e.g., Django/Commons validators), enforce numeric/date parsing with exceptions, check min/max ranges and lengths, and restrict string parameters to predefined allowed values.

Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: FileSearch
  description: An API for checking if a file with given content or name exists on the server
  version: 1.0.11
paths:
  /search:
    post:
      summary: Retreive a list of files from the server that contain the specified content or match the filename.
      description: The server stores files in the /data directory. This endpoint will return a list of complete paths to files in data that contain the specified content or start. It is possible to specify a relative path in search_dir.
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              properties:
                search_content:
                  type: string | null
                  example: Hello World
                search_filename:
                  type: string | null
                  example: file.txt
                search_dir:
                  type: string | null
                  example: /songs
      responses:
        '200':
          description: List of files that contain the specified content or match the filename. (or empty list if none found)
          content:
            application/json:
                schema:
                    type: object
                    properties:
                        files:
                            type: array
                            items:
                                type: string
                            example: ["/data/files/file1.txt", "/data/songs/song.mp3"]
        '400':
          description: Invalid input

The server's purpose is to provide an API that allows users to check if a file with a given content or name exists on the server.
It exposes a single POST API endpoint, which is "/search".
When making a request to this endpoint, the user must provide a JSON object in the request body with two optional parameters: "search_content" and "search_filename".
The "search_content" parameter is a string that represents the content to search for within the files, and the "search_filename" parameter is a string that represents the name of the file to search for.
Both parameters can be null if not used.
The "search_dir" parameter is an optional string that represents the relative path to search for files in. If not provided, the search will be performed in the data root directory.
The server searches for files in the data root "/data" directory on its local file system.
If the request is successful, the server responds with a status code of 200 and returns a JSON object containing a "files" field. This "files" field is an array of strings, where each string is a complete path to a file in the "/data" directory that either contains the specified content or matches the specified filename.
If the input is invalid, the server responds with a status code of 400.

sec_guidelines.group_name: Improper Input Validation and Path Traversal
sec_guidelines.guidelines:
1. **Input Validation**: Validate the `search_dir` input to prevent path traversal attacks. Ensure it only contains allowed characters and does not include `..` or other directory traversal sequences. Example:
   ```javascript
   if (!/^[a-zA-Z0-9/_-]*$/.test(search_dir)) throw new Error('Invalid directory');
   ```
2. **Path Sanitization**: Use `path.basename()` to sanitize the filename and directory inputs before using them in file operations. This prevents unauthorized access to files outside the intended directory. Example:

Input Validation and File Upload Security
WHAT: Failure to strictly validate user input and uploaded files (e.g., unbounded length, arbitrary characters, user-controlled filenames/paths, unsafe types) can allow XSS, path traversal, malicious file execution, or resource exhaustion.
WHY: Attackers can bypass client-side checks, inject scripts, upload executable or oversized files, and gain unauthorized access or execute arbitrary code.
HOW: Enforce server-side allowlist validation for all inputs (characters, format, min/max length); use context-appropriate output encoding for all user-controlled data; restrict upload types/extensions and size; never trust user-supplied filenames or paths—generate server-side names and fixed storage paths; pre-validate ZIP contents (target path, compression level, estimated size) and scan uploads with security tools.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java, unsafe): `String zip = request.getParameter("zip"); process(zip);` After: `if (!zipPattern.matcher(zip).matches()) throw new ValidationException();` and for uploads: reject disallowed extensions, rename to a random server-generated filename, store under a fixed directory, and serve with the correct content-type.

Path traversal and unsafe file/URL handling
WHAT: User-controlled filename or URL parameters are used directly for file upload/download paths or redirects, allowing `../` path traversal or arbitrary external redirects.
WHY: Attackers can read/write files outside the intended directory (e.g., `.env` with credentials) or trick users into phishing sites via open redirects.
HOW: For file paths, strip directory components with `basename()` and enforce allowlists or per-user directories; never concatenate raw user input into paths. For redirects, validate URLs against an allowlist or restrict to same-origin paths before redirecting.
EXAMPLE: Before (vulnerable): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').$request->input('filename'));` After (safer): `response()->download(storage_path('content/').basename($request->input('filename')));`

Error Handling and Information Disclosure
WHAT: Unhandled or improperly handled errors that return stack traces, SQL errors, file paths, or technology/version details to clients, instead of a generic error response.
WHY: Such detailed error messages aid attackers in reconnaissance, help identify injection points, and expose internal implementation details that increase exploitability.
HOW: Configure a global error handler to catch unexpected exceptions, log full details only on the server, and return a generic, implementation-agnostic error response (e.g., HTTP 5xx with RFC 7807-compliant body) that reveals no stack traces, queries, or paths.
EXAMPLE: Before (Java web.xml): no `<error-page>` mapping, default container error pages show stack traces. After: add `<error-page><exception-type>java.lang.Exception</exception-type><location>/error.jsp</location></error-page>` and implement `error.jsp` to log the exception server-side and return a generic error message to the client.

Hide detailed error information from clients
WHAT: Returning full error details or stack traces to clients (e.g., via default error handlers) exposes internal paths, modules, and workflows.
WHY: Attackers can use this information to map the system, discover technologies in use, and craft targeted exploits.
HOW: In production, configure a centralized error handler that logs full errors server-side but returns only generic messages and appropriate HTTP status codes to clients; ensure environment flags (e.g., NODE_ENV) are set correctly.
EXAMPLE: Before (Express, leaking stack): `app.use(errorHandler());` with default dev config; After: `app.use((err, req, res, next) => { console.error(err); res.status(err.status||500).json({error:'Internal server error'}); });`

text_spec:
The server is designed to support a simple web application called MyForum, which allows users to post and read messages. It exposes two API endpoints.

The first endpoint is a GET request at the path "/messages", which retrieves all previously posted messages. The response for this request is in the format of a string with a content type of "text/html".
This endpoint accepts three optional query parameters: "limit", "offset", and "sort". The "limit" parameter specifies the number of messages to return, the "offset" parameter specifies the number of messages to skip before starting to collect the result set, and the "sort" parameter specifies the sorting direction of the messages. The "sort" parameter can have two values: "ASC" for ascending order and "DESC" for descending order. The response to a successful request has a status code of 200.

The second endpoint is a POST request at the same path "/messages", which allows users to post a new message to the forum. This request requires a JSON object in the request body, which must conform to the "Message" schema. The "Message" schema is defined as an object with a single property named "content", which is a string. An example value for "content" is "hello world!". The POST request can result in two possible responses: a "200" status code indicating a successful operation or a "400" status code indicating invalid input.
